Putting greens for Windermere's golf-community lots

A backyard putting green in Windermere runs $14–$30 per square foot installed, typically $18–$25, as of September 2026. Isleworth, Keene's Pointe and the Reserve at Lake Butler Sound are built around golf courses, which makes a home green a natural fit, and also means an architectural committee reviews it first.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Why a green fits a golf-community lot

Isleworth, Keene's Pointe and Lake Butler Sound were platted around golf courses from the start, so a homeowner already living beside a fairway is a more common candidate for a home putting green than someone on a standard suburban lot elsewhere in our service area. A contoured green with two or three cups and a chipping pad reads as an extension of the course view rather than an unusual addition, which is part of why the request comes up more often here than in a typical subdivision.

That same fairway view is also what draws the closest architectural scrutiny, since a green sits in the most visible part of many of these lots.

What a putting green quote should itemize separately

A Windermere putting green quote worth comparing against another bid lists the deeper excavation and hand-shaping labor, fiber type, cup count and hardware, and infill rate as separate lines rather than one flat per-square-foot number the way a lawn quote often can. Two of those items, the shaping labor and cup hardware, don't scale simply with square footage the way turf material does, so a small, heavily contoured green can cost more per square foot than a larger, simpler one. Asking for those lines broken out shows which part of the price is actually paying for the design work versus the turf itself.

Say you have an 800 sq ft green and fringe near a Keene's Pointe fairway

An 800 sq ft putting green with fringe, set back from a Keene's Pointe fairway line by the community's standard rear setback, runs $14–$30 per square foot, or about $11,200 to $24,000 at the published range depending on contouring and cup count. A two-cup layout with modest breaks lands toward the lower half of that range; a three-cup green with a chipping pad and more elaborate shaping pushes toward the top.

An ARC application with the green's footprint and a turf sample goes in before the crew is scheduled, and the review typically takes longer than the install itself, since these committees weigh a fairway-facing feature more carefully than an interior side-yard change.

What an ARC submittal for a green needs

None of the three communities publishes a synthetic-turf clause we could find and cite, so a putting green submittal goes in as a general landscape or hardscape change: a site sketch showing the green's footprint and contours, a sample of the product, and a description of the fringe and cup placement. Because Florida’s HOA statute protects a change only if it isn't visible from the street or an adjacent lot, and a fairway-facing green usually is visible from somewhere, the ARC review carries more weight here than the state's own turf standard does for this particular decision.

What a green retrofit risks hitting underground

Cutting out an established Windermere lawn to make room for a green's deeper four- to six-inch excavation risks striking an old irrigation line that was capped at the valve when the original lawn went in, since a line that no longer waters anything doesn't always get marked or remembered years later. Confirming where any capped zones ran before digging avoids severing a line that, while inactive, may still be tied into the broader irrigation system serving the rest of the property. A quick check with whoever handled the original lawn conversion, or a look at the valve box layout, settles this before the first shovel of a retrofit goes in.

Why washed rock matters more under a putting surface

The same rule requiring washed rock under any Windermere lawn applies to a putting green's base, and the consequences of skipping it show up faster here than almost anywhere else on the property. Fines from unwashed fill binding into a crust don't just slow drainage the way they would under a lawn; they also create an uneven surface underneath the shaped tiers, which shows up as a dead spot or an unexpected bounce exactly where a ball should be rolling true. A green's fine tolerance for surface consistency makes a crusted, uneven base far more noticeable in daily use than the same problem would be under grass nobody's testing with a putter.

Base work on a lake-ridge lot

The deep, fast-draining Candler-family sand common on Windermere's lake-ridge lots holds a shaped subbase well, since it doesn't stay saturated the way flatter flatwoods soil can after a summer storm (USDA’s official series description). Contouring a green into that sand still calls for the same washed, open-graded crushed rock as any other job, built up in shaped lifts rather than a flat pass, so a subtle rise-and-fall reads true when a ball rolls across it.

A shaped green built into ridge sand isn't unique to Windermere's golf communities; Dr. Phillips, Winter Garden and Ocoee all carry lots worth the same look, and our cost breakdown for greens across Central Florida explains how contouring moves the price within the published range. The putting green service page has more on cup and fringe options.

Setting cups once the base is fully shaped

Cups go in after the Windermere green's base has been shaped, compacted, and confirmed to hold its breaks, cored through at the design's marked locations rather than positioned by eye during installation. Each cup gets set and edged individually, which takes longer per hole than any other single step in building a green, since a slightly crooked or poorly seated cup stands out immediately against a surface built for precision. Waiting until the base is finished before coring also avoids having to patch a cup location that turns out to sit in the wrong spot once the shape is complete.

Brushing a green to keep the roll consistent

Consistency in a Windermere green's roll comes far more from regular grooming than from the age of the surface itself, which is why a light pass with a stiff brush, moving opposite the nap direction, belongs on a repeating schedule rather than a once-a-year task. Skipping several months between brushings lets the fiber settle into whatever direction foot traffic and rain have pushed it, and a ball crossing that section starts to pull slightly off line even though nothing about the green looks different to the eye. A gentle, frequent touch keeps the surface predictable in a way that one thorough grooming a year never quite manages.

Questions people ask

Do Windermere's golf communities allow synthetic putting greens?

We found no published ARC document from Isleworth, Keene's Pointe or Lake Butler Sound that names synthetic turf or putting greens specifically. A submittal with a sample and a site plan through the community's standard review process is how to find out for a given lot.

How is the best backyard putting green near a Windermere fairway actually planned?

Start with how the green will read next to the golf course itself: matching mow height and green speed to a natural look matters more here than in a yard with no course view at all. Beyond that, the same checklist applies everywhere: named base depth, product face weight, and cup placement in writing before work starts.
